clinicalPearls: An inherited thrombophilia in which reduced antithrombin activity removes a key brake on coagulation, producing a strong predisposition to venous thromboembolism
Among the heritable thrombophilias it confers one of the highest relative risks of thrombosis, often presenting at a young age or in unusual sites such as mesenteric or cerebral veins
Thrombosis is frequently provoked by additional risk factors including pregnancy, the postpartum period, surgery, immobility, and oestrogen-containing contraception
A characteristic clue is apparent resistance to unfractionated heparin, because heparin works by potentiating antithrombin, which is deficient
Diagnosis uses a functional antithrombin activity assay; levels can be lowered acutely by active clot, heparin therapy, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, and disseminated intravascular coagulation
Testing is best deferred until after the acute event and away from anticoagulant interference to avoid misclassification, and family screening is worthwhile
Acute venous thromboembolism is treated with anticoagulation, and antithrombin concentrate may be used in high-risk situations such as surgery or delivery when heparin alone is inadequate
Long-term anticoagulation is considered after unprovoked or recurrent thrombosis given the high recurrence risk
reference.pathophysiology: Antithrombin is a circulating serine protease inhibitor that neutralises thrombin and factor Xa (and other activated clotting factors), acting as a principal natural anticoagulant; its activity is greatly accelerated by heparin and endothelial heparan sulphate. Inherited deficiency, usually autosomal dominant, arises from mutations that reduce either the amount (type I) or the function (type II) of the protein. With less effective inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa, coagulation proceeds unchecked, tipping haemostatic balance towards thrombosis. Acquired reductions occur through loss (nephrotic syndrome), reduced synthesis (liver disease), or consumption (acute thrombosis, DIC, heparin therapy).
additionalDifferentials: Factor V Leiden and activated protein C resistance
Acquired antithrombin loss (nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, DIC)
additionalInvestigations: Functional antithrombin activity assay as the key diagnostic test
Antithrombin antigen level to distinguish type I from type II deficiency
A broader thrombophilia panel (protein C, protein S, factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid antibodies)
Repeat testing away from acute thrombosis and heparin therapy to confirm a persistent defect
Renal and liver assessment to exclude acquired causes
Family testing of first-degree relatives once a hereditary defect is confirmed
redFlags: Acute venous thromboembolism, including extensive deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
Thrombosis at unusual sites such as cerebral, mesenteric, or hepatic veins
Apparent heparin resistance with failure to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation
Pregnancy or the peripartum period, when thrombotic risk is greatly increased and needs proactive management
reference.prognosis: Antithrombin deficiency carries a high lifetime and recurrence risk of venous thromboembolism relative to other inherited thrombophilias; with appropriate anticoagulation, risk-situation prophylaxis, and use of antithrombin concentrate when indicated, most affected individuals can be managed effectively.
pitfalls: Interpreting a low antithrombin level measured during acute thrombosis or heparin therapy as hereditary deficiency without confirmatory repeat testing
Failing to recognise heparin resistance as a clue to the diagnosis
Overlooking acquired causes such as nephrotic syndrome or liver disease
Not providing intensified prophylaxis or antithrombin support during pregnancy, surgery, or delivery
Omitting family counselling and screening after a hereditary defect is identified
